questionStem: A 20-year-old woman , gravida 1, para 0, at 36 weeks' gestation delivers a stillborn infant. She had no prenatal care, and the prenatal course was complicated by maternal cocaine and alcohol use. She also was seen in the emergency department at 20 weeks' gestation after being assaulted by her boyfriend . Examination at the time showed scalp and forearm lacerations and bruising of the abdomen and face . She took phenytoin during the pregnancy for a seizure disorder ; she had no seizures during the pregnancy . An autopsy of the fetus shows multiple fractures of thin ribs and multiple fractures of the rather broad and ribbon-shaped tubular bones. Examination of the fetus shows blue sclerae , soft calvaria , a small chest, and bent short extremities . Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of this condition?

choices.C: Intrauterine trauma resulting from abuse to the mother

correctExplanation: This infant likely died from complications of osteogenesis imperfecta, which results from mutations or posttranslational defects in collagen, type I. Given the presence of collagen, type I, in bone, skin, and connective tissues, pathology results from connective tissue defects ranging in severity from postpubertal fractures to fatal fractures in utero. The presentation of this fetus likely reflects fragile long bones along with decreased calvarial ossification and thin sclerae (leading to visualization of the choroidal veins). Patients may also present with short stature, scoliosis, basilar skull deformities (leading to nerve compression), hearing loss (likely related to abnormal bone formation in the ossicles and cochlea), opalescent and fragile teeth, and easy bruising (caused by collagen, type I, defects in blood vessel walls). Treatment is primarily supportive, involving possible bisphosphonates along with monitoring for complications, physical therapy, and genetic counseling.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Alcohol-induced fetal abnormalities (Choice B) include intellectual disability, developmental delay, and physical malformations such as microcephaly, facial dysmorphia, limb deformities, and congenital heart disease. Patients with fetal alcohol syndrome may demonstrate abnormal bone development (eg, cervical spine fusion) and delayed bone growth. However, osseous fragility would be atypical. Intrauterine trauma resulting from abuse to the mother (Choice C) may lead to increased fetal cortisol production and stress physiology. However, in the absence of a blunt or penetrating injury to the mother, mechanical trauma to the fetus would be unlikely. Placental insufficiency from cocaine use (Choice D) can lead to preterm birth, intrauterine growth restriction, low birth weight, and placental abruption. However, osseous fragility would be atypical. Teratogenicity of phenytoin (Choice E) commonly causes orofacial clefts, cardiac malformations, and genitourinary defects. In adults, phenytoin may cause osteomalacia as a result of changes in calcium metabolism. However, maternal phenytoin use is unlikely to result in osseous fragility in infants. Educational Objective: In osteogenesis imperfecta, abnormalities of collagen, type I, lead to connective tissue defects and consequent bone fractures, scoliosis, short stature, skull deformities, blue sclera, fragile teeth, hearing loss, and easy bruising. Severe cases lead to death in utero. " , ~ F' r ,

questionStem: A previously healthy 1-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of a 2-month history of increasing weakness and difficulty feeding . He is alert. Examination shows tongue fasciculations and profound hypotonia . Deep tendon reflexes are absent. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: This patient most likely has progressive infantile spinal muscular atrophy (SMA). SMA commonly involves an autosomal recessive mutation of the SMN protein, resulting in defective mRNA synthesis in motor neurons. The infantile form of SMA typically affects normally developing infants who are several months old. In spinal muscular atrophy, the bilateral lower brainstem motor nuclei and anterior horns degenerate, leading to progressive, symmetric muscular weakness and a lower motor neuron-pattern of dysfunction (eg, decreased tone, hyporeflexia, fasciculations, early-onset atrophy). The lower extremities are typically more affected than the upper extremities. Dysfunction progresses over the course of months. In severe cases, progressive respiratory insufficiency may develop. The diagnosis can be confirmed with genetic testing. Treatment is supportive and includes promoting nutrition, motor, and respiratory function.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Botulism (Choice A) is an acute disease of the neuromuscular junction caused by the exposure to the C/ostridium botulinum toxin (eg, in raw honey). Over the course of hours to days, patients develop symmetric hypotonia and hyporeflexia that begins with the cranial nerves and descends to the lower extremities in a presentation that may mimic SMA. However, this patient's weakness developed over the course of months rather than hours to days. Guillain-Barre syndrome (Choice B) results from the autoimmune attack of the spinal nerve roots and typically presents with acute-onset, symmetric, ascending muscle weakness with hyporeflexia. This patient's weakness instead progressed over months. Many patients also demonstrate autonomic dysfunction and/or sensory symptoms, which would be atypical in SMA. Myasthenia gravis (Choice C) is an autoimmune disorder of neuromuscular transmission that may result in focal or generalized muscle weakness and fatigability. Myasthenia gravis demonstrates a bimodal age of onset in both young adults (teens to 20s) and older adults (50s to 60s). Myasthenia gravis in an infant would be atypical. Transverse myelitis (Choice E) is an acquired condition in which inflammation (eg, from an infection or autoimmune disease) affects one section of the spinal cord bilaterally, leading to acute motor, sensory, or autonomic dysfunction. This patient instead experienced the insidious onset of motor dysfunction only. Educational Objective: In spinal muscular atrophy, the bilateral lower brainstem motor nuclei and anterior horns degenerate, leading to progressive, symmetric muscular weakness and a lower motor neuron-pattern of dysfunction (eg, decreased tone, hyporeflexia, fasciculations, early-onset atrophy). Deficits typically progress during the course of months, which differentiates spinal muscular atrophy from the acute descending motor weakness of botulism. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: An asymptomatic 10-year-old boy is brought to the physician for a well-child examination . He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications . His parents both have essential hypertension and hyperlipidemia . He has an active lifestyle and plays several sports. He consumes a wide variety of foods , including meat, fruit, and vegetables , and drinks two to three glasses each of whole milk and fruit juice daily. He is currently at the 75th percentile for height and above the 97th percentile for weight and BMI. Vital signs are within normal limits. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's current weight?

choices.D: Inadequate intake of fruits and vegetables

correctExplanation: In children, overweight is defined as a BMI at or above the 85th percentile and below the 95th percentile for age and gender, while obesity is defined as a BMI at or above the 95th percentile. This obese child consumes a balanced diet but one that most likely contains excessive total calories. Common causes of childhood obesity include consuming a diet rich in unhealthy, calorie-rich foods, and a lack of sufficient exercise. Children from socioeconomically disadvantaged communities may face significant difficulties in obtaining healthy food and sufficient opportunity for exercise. Children with obesity are more likely to develop comorbidities such as hypertension and diabetes mellitus.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Excessive intake of carbohydrates (Choice A) and excessive intake of fat (Choice B) are both correct but insufficient to explain this child's obesity. This child consumes a balanced diet as well as several glasses of both milk and fruit juice daily and is likely consuming an excess of both carbohydrates and fat, as well as protein. Inadequate intake of fruits and vegetables (Choice D) may lead to obesity indirectly by causing a child to consume an unhealthy diet that favors fatty or salty foods instead. This child does not have a history of consuming inadequate fruits or vegetables. Inadequate physical activity (Choice E) is a common cause of obesity in children. This child has an active lifestyle and his diet is a more likely cause of his obesity. Educational Objective: In children, overweight is defined as a BMI at or above the 85th percentile and below the 95th percentile for age and gender, while obesity is defined as a BMI at or above the 95th percentile. Common causes of childhood obesity include consuming an excessive amount of total calories, a diet rich in unhealthy, calorie-rich foods, and a lack of sufficient exercise. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 3-week-old boy is brought to the physician 4 hours after the onset of vomiting watery, green material. His mother says that he has been drawing up his legs as if in pain while vomiting . He appears uncomfortable . He is afebrile . The abdomen is tender but not distended. An abdominal x-ray shows dilated loops of small bowel and air-fluid levels . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Volvulus occurs when a portion of the gastrointestinal tract twists, leading to bowel obstruction. Midgut volvulus usually occurs in children who have intestinal malrotation, a congenital anomaly in which the midgut incompletely rotates during development, and typically presents within the first year of life. The most common initial symptom in infants is vomiting, which becomes bilious as a result of the blockage of the small bowel and the retrograde flow of bile. In older children, abdominal pain is the most common presenting symptom. The diagnosis can be confirmed with imaging. Plain x-rays are acquired first to screen for perforation. Once perforation has been excluded, an upper gastrointestinal contrast series is obtained. Imaging studies may show evidence of malrotation with a small bowel obstruction including air-fluid levels and dilated loops of bowel. If not recognized quickly, volvulus can lead to vascular compromise with subsequent intestinal necrosis, perforation, and peritonitis.
incorrectExplanation: nd I. Appendicitis {Choice A) typically presents with right lower quadrant abdominal pain that is often periumbilical at onset, along with nausea, anorexia, fever, leukocytosis, and tenderness to palpation in the right lower quadrant on examination. It does not cause bowel obstruction or bilious vomiting. Congenital megacolon (Hirschsprung disease) {Choice B), also known as intestinal aganglionosis, is caused by the congenital absence of the distal portion of the myenteric plexus. This often leads to an inability to pass meconium within the first few days of life and may result in a large bowel obstruction. An explosive expulsion of feces on rectal examination is a classic clinical finding. Duodenal atresia {Choice C) is caused by failure of recanalization of the duodenal lumen. Duodenal atresia presents with vomiting and abdominal distension, as well as gaseous dilation of the stomach and duodenum on an abdominal x-ray. Foreign body ingestion {Choice D) may cause intestinal obstruction and bilious vomiting. However, it is more common in older infants and toddlers who tend to put items in their mouths, not 3-week-old newborns. In an infant, gastroesophageal reflux disease {Choice E) presents with frequent regurgitation without excessive irritability. Bilious vomiting is a warning sign of a structural cause of vomiting. Hepatitis {Choice F) can be caused by viral infections, autoimmune diseases, or medications. Hyperbilirubinemia with jaundice or icterus is often present. It is not a cause of small bowel obstruction or bilious vomiting. lntussusception {Choice G) occurs when an intestinal lead point causes the small or large intestine to telescope on itself. It presents with episodic, crampy abdominal pain accompanied by crying, vomiting, and bloody, mucoid stool. Pancreatitis {Choice H) presents with epigastric abdominal pain that radiates to the back, along with nausea and emesis. Acute pancreatitis can be complicated by necrosis, hemorrhage, abscess, or the formation of pseudocysts, but generally not a small bowel obstruction. Pyloric stenosis {Choice I) is caused by hypertrophy of the pyloric sphincter, leading to gastric outlet obstruction and vomiting. It commonly presents with non bloody, nonbilious emesis after feedings, and begins around 3 to 6 weeks of age. Educational Objective: Congenital malrotation of the intestines predisposes to midgut volvulus, which presents with signs of small bowel obstruction including bilious vomiting and abdominal distension. X-ray findings of small bowel obstruction include dilated loops of bowel with air-fluid levels. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A previously healthy 6-month-old boy is admitted to the hospital because of a 1-day history of fever, lethargy, and vomiting. His temperature is 39°C (102.2°F), pulse is 160/min, and respirations are 34/min. Examination shows nuchal rigidity and a bulging anterior fontanel. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin 12.2 g/dL Leukocyte count 17,300/mm 3 Platelet count 262,000/mm 3 Serum Na + K+ Cl· HC0 3- Glucose 121 mEq/L 4.2 mEq/L 105 mEq/L 16 mEq/L 150 mg/dL Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's serum sodium concentration?

choices.C: Increased loss of chloride in the kidneys
choices.D: Increased secretion of ADH vaso ressin)

correctExplanation: Fever, lethargy, vomiting, altered mental status, nuchal rigidity, and a bulging anterior fontanel raise suspicion for meningitis. This patient's hyponatremia is likely caused by syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH). Release of ADH (vasopressin) by the posterior pituitary is typically stimulated by an increase in plasma osmolality but can also occur without stimulus in the setting of SIADH. SIADH can occur as an adverse effect of medications (eg, cyclophosphamide), a paraneoplastic process, or secondary to a central nervous system disorder (eg, stroke, hemorrhage, infection, trauma, or tumor). In this patient, the cause of SIADH is likely a result of meningitis. Treatment of hyponatremia involves treatment of any underlying disease and gradual sodium correction, typically with fluid restriction. A safe rate of sodium correction is generally no more than 6 to 12 mEq/day. When hyponatremia is corrected too rapidly, extracellular sodium exerts osmotic pressure that leads to the rapid efflux of water from neurons, which can lead to demyelination. The pons is particularly vulnerable to demyelinating injury and the rapid correction of hyponatremia can result in central pontine myelinolysis.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Excessive intake of free water (Choice A) can occur with psychogenic polydipsia, resulting in dilute urine and hyponatremia. It would be unlikely in this patient presenting with meningitis, and the cause of hyponatremia is more likely a result of SIADH. Factitious hyponatremia due to hyperglycemia (Choice B) can occur in patients with severe hyperglycemia. This patient's glucose is 150 mg/dL, which would not be enough to cause hyponatremia on laboratory evaluation. Severe hyperglycemia can lead to the osmotic shift of water from the intracellular to extracellular space, leading to dilutional hyponatremia in the serum. Increased loss of chloride in the kidneys (Choice C) would not explain this patient's hyponatremia. Chloride is typically reabsorbed with sodium in the nephron. The patient's hyponatremia is not caused by abnormalities of sodium or chloride reabsorption or excretion, but rather, increased free water reabsorption as a result of SIADH. The patient's chloride concentration is normal. Insufficient intake of sodium chloride (Choice E) would not itself cause hyponatremia as a result of the kidney's ability to reabsorb sodium and water to maintain a homeostatic serum osmolarity. SIADH impairs this ability by causing unregulated free water reabsorption. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 25-year-old woman , gravida 2, para 1, at 20 weeks' gestation comes to the physician for a routine prenatal visit. She feels well, and her pregnancy has been uncomplicated . Examination shows a uterus consistent in size with a 20-week gestation . She reports that her first child had bloody diarrhea as an infant when he was fed cow milk-based formula . The diarrhea resolved when the formula was changed to a hypoallergenic type . She states that she avoids dairy products because they upset her stomach . She asks how she can prevent food allergies in her next child. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation ?

choices.A: Delay the introduction of solid food until the age of 9 months
choices.B: Do not feed the infant eggs or peanut-based products until the age of 9 months
choices.C: Exclusively breast-feed for at least 6 months
choices.D: Use a hypoallergenic formula for at least 6 months
choices.E: Use a lactose-free formula exclusively for at least 9 months

correctExplanation: Food allergies are a component of the atopic triad, which consists of atopic dermatitis, asthma, and food or environmental allergies. Food allergies may be immunoglobulin E (lgE)-mediated (eg, urticaria, angioedema, anaphylaxis) or non-lgE-mediated (eg, food protein-induced proctitis, proctocolitis, enterocolitis). Exclusive breast-feeding for at least 6 months is hypothesized to decrease the rate of food allergy in infants. Dietary avoidance of allergenic foods during pregnancy or lactation does not lead to decreased rates of food allergies in children. In actuality, introducing allergenic foods into the diet while lactating may lead to an increased likelihood of tolerance developing in the child and decreased rates of food allergy.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Delaying the introduction of solid food (Choice A) or delaying introduction of allergenic foods including eggs and peanut-based products (Choice B) until the age of 9 months has not been shown to decrease rates of food allergy. In contrast, the early introduction of allergenic foods has been recommended in order to improve tolerance to these foods. Use of a hypoallergenic formula for at least 6 months (Choice D) or a lactose-free formula for at least 9 months (Choice E) is not necessary nor shown to decrease food allergy development. In contrast, exclusive breast-feeding for at least 6 months is recommended. At 6 months, solid foods can begin to be introduced. Educational Objective: Exclusive breast-feeding for at least 6 months is hypothesized to decrease the rate of food allergy in infants. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 15-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 3-day history of severe pain and swelling in her right sternoclavicular joint. Ten days ago, the patient had a sore throat. She has no history of serious illness and takes no medications . Her temperature is 40°C (104 °F). Examination shows erythema , swelling , and tenderness of the right sternoclavicular joint. Aspiration of the affected joint yields thick , yellow, purulent fluid . A Gram stain of the fluid shows numerous segmented neutrophils and numerous gram-negative diplococci. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.D: CT scan of the left sternoclavicular joint

correctExplanation: This patient with monoarticular septic arthritis of the sternoclavicular joint from disseminated infection with Neisseria gonorrhoeae should undergo arthrocentesis with culture of the aspirate fluid. Septic arthritis commonly occurs in children as a result of trauma to the joint permitting the translocation of cutaneous organisms (eg, Staphylococcus aureus) and may also occur in adolescents as a result of the dissemination of Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection. Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a sexually transmitted bacterium that initially causes cervicitis, urethritis, or pharyngitis and may hematogenously disseminate to cause septic arthritis. Septic arthritis classically presents with a painful, erythematous, swollen joint along with systemic signs and symptoms of illness such as fever, chills, myalgia, arthralgia, and nausea. Gonococcal arthritis may present with monoarticular or asymmetric polyarticular disease and may feature adjacent tenosynovitis and dermatitis. The most common sites of gonococcal infection are the knee, ankle, wrist, and elbow, though the sternoclavicular joint may also be affected. In all causes of septic arthritis, serum laboratory values typically show leukocytosis along with increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein concentrations. Diagnosis requires arthrocentesis, which typically demonstrates purulent aspirate fluid with an increased concentration of neutrophil-predominant white blood cells. In gonococcal arthritis, culture of the aspirate fluid may disclose gram-negative diplococci. Management requires antibiotic therapy with ceftriaxone and azithromycin along with source control.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Chest x-ray (Choice B) may be used to detect late findings of underlying osteomyelitis (eg, erosions) in patients with septic arthritis caused by the translocation of cutaneous organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus. However, osteomyelitis is less likely to result from gonococcal arthritis. Echocardiography (Choice C) would be helpful in diagnosing gonococcal endocarditis, a rare complication of disseminated Neisseria gonorrhoeae infection. However, this patient with symptoms localized to a joint most likely has gonococcal arthritis. CT scan of the left sternoclavicular joint (Choice D) may assist in the visualization of a joint effusion. This is especially true in difficult-to-examine joints such as the hip. However, joint aspiration is the preferred method for definitively diagnosing septic arthritis. Indium-labeled leukocyte scan (Choice E), a nuclear medicine procedure that adds a radioactive tag to white blood cells, assists in localizing sites of infection and inflammation, and is often used in patients with a fever of unknown origin. This patient possesses a clear source of infection. Educational Objective: Neisseria gonorrhoeae is a sexually transmitted bacterium that initially causes cervicitis, urethritis, or pharyngitis, and may hematogenously disseminate to cause septic arthritis. Gonococcal arthritis may present with monoarticular or asymmetric polyarticular erythema, edema, and tenderness. Diagnosis requires culture of the aspirate synovial fluid, which typically demonstrates gram-negative diplococci and an increased concentration of neutrophil-predominant white blood cells. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 9-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of headache and dizziness for the past week . She has a history of recurrent urinary tract infections . At the age of 2 years , she received the diagnosis of vesicoureteral reflux and was treated with prophylactic amoxicillin until the age of 6 years . She has been admitted to the hospital twice for treatment of pyelonephritis . Development is appropriate for age , and her immunizations are up-to-date. Her height and weight are below the 5th percentile . Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 80/min , respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 160/100 mm Hg in all four extremities . Funduscopic examination shows narrowing of the retinal arteries . Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.A: Follow-up blood pressure measurement in 1 week
choices.C: Measurement of serum urea nitrogen and creatinine concentrations

correctExplanation: Measurement of serum urea nitrogen and creatinine concentrations is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis. This patient with chronic vesicoureteral reflux and a history of recurrent pyelonephritis with new onset headache and dizziness in the setting of hypertension most likely has hypertensive urgency that has developed as a result of chronic kidney disease. Chronic vesicoureteral reflux predisposes patients to the development of recurrent pyelonephritis as urine from the bladder travels in a retrograde fashion to the kidneys. Recurrent pyelonephritis can lead to scarring of the renal parenchyma and loss of nephron mass, which decreases the glomerular filtration rate, and can lead to chronic kidney disease. Hypertension is a common complication of chronic renal disease and results primarily from impaired handling of sodium leading to expansion of the intravascular volume and subsequent systolic hypertension. Over time, chronic vascular remodeling and increased systemic vascular resistance lead to an increase in diastolic blood pressure. Assessment of the serum urea nitrogen and creatinine concentrations is an appropriate first step in assessing kidney function. Increases in both are suggestive of kidney injury. Further assessment of urinary protein excretion is also appropriate.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Follow-up blood pressure measurement in 1 week (Choice A) is not appropriate at this time. The patient is presenting with symptoms, including headache and dizziness, that may be attributed to her hypertension. Further workup to determine the cause of her hypertension with simultaneous treatment is necessary. Blood cultures (Choice B) are not necessary. The patient is afebrile and has no flank pain or dysuria, making the diagnosis of acute pyelonephritis unlikely. Thyroid function tests (Choice D) are typically completed in the evaluation of secondary hypertension but would not be the first step. Hypothyroidism is more commonly associated with hypertension than hyperthyroidism, but patients also typically present with weight gain, constipation, fatigue, and cold intolerance. CT scan of the head (Choice E) should be considered in patients with focal neurologic deficits or severe, sudden onset headache, to rule out hemorrhagic stroke or subarachnoid hemorrhage. This patient has had a headache for 1 week and has no neurologic deficits reported; a CT scan would likely provide little additional diagnostic information and would not be the best next step. Educational Objective: Chronic vesicoureteral reflux predisposes patients to recurrent pyelonephritis, which can result in scarring of the renal parenchyma and loss of nephron mass leading to chronic kidney disease. Impaired salt handling in chronic renal disease leads to expansion of the intravascular volume and subsequent hypertension. Laboratory evaluation should include the measurement of serum urea nitrogen and creatinine concentrations. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A previously healthy 16-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 4-month history of progressive fatigue and nervousness , intermittent blurred vision , and declining school performance . She has had a 3-kg (6.6-lb) weight loss during this period despite an increased appetite . Her sister has hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine . The patient's temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 110/80 mm Hg. Examination shows warm flushed skin and fine soft hair. There is mild exophthalmos and lid lag. Funduscopic examination and visual fields show no abnormalities . Examination of the neck shows an enlarged thyroid gland with a bruit. There is a fine tremor when her upper extremities are outstretched . Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's findings?

choices.B: Lymphocytic infiltration of the thyroid gland
choices.C: Malignant infiltration of the thyroid gland

correctExplanation: Graves disease is an autoimmune hyperthyroid condition caused by thyroid-stimulating autoantibodies that activate the thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) receptor. Hyperstimulation of the TSH receptor leads to overproduction of thyroid hormone and a diffusely enlarged thyroid gland on physical examination, along with signs and symptoms of hyperthyroidism including weight loss, insomnia, palpitations, heat intolerance, warm skin, tremor, diaphoresis, and pretibial myxedema. TSH-receptor-stimulating antibodies also stimulate orbital fibroblasts and lead to thyroid ophthalmopathy, which is characterized by the expansion of orbital fat and connective tissue with resultant exophthalmos, lid lag, and restrictive strabismus. Thyroid ophthalmopathy may lead to diplopia, corneal exposure, compressive optic neuropathy, and a cosmetic appearance that is distressing for patients. Thyroid laboratory studies typically demonstrate primary hyperthyroidism with increased thyroxine and triiodothyronine, and decreased TSH. Radioactive iodine uptake nuclear scintigraphy typically demonstrates diffuse, abnormally increased uptake of the thyroid gland without a discrete nodule. Graves disease is treated with antithyroid drugs such as methimazole and propylthiouracil, and radioactive iodine ablation of the thyroid gland. Thyroid ophthalmopathy typically responds well to topical lubrication, although severe cases may require intravenous corticosteroids and a staged surgical approach.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Levothyroxine overdose (Choice A) may present with signs and symptoms of hyperthyroidism including tachycardia, hypertension, tremor, and anxiety. Severe cases may cause convulsions and coma. This patient's history of progressive symptoms over a four-month period, as well as her symptoms of exophthalmos and lid lag, are not consistent with an overdose event. Lymphocytic infiltration of the thyroid gland (Choice B) is characteristic of Hashimoto disease. While patients with Hashimoto disease may present with transient symptoms of hyperthyroidism during the acute stage, patients progress to develop signs and symptoms of hypothyroidism, including fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, hyporeflexia, myxedema, and dry, cool skin. Hashimoto disease does not cause orbital findings of exophthalmos and lid lag. Malignant infiltration of the thyroid gland (Choice C) may lead to symptoms of hyperthyroidism through the destruction of thyroid follicular cells with resultant release of thyroid hormone, though patients are generally euthyroid. This mechanism would not cause orbital findings of exophthalmos and lid lag. Thyroid-stimulating hormone-producing pituitary tumor (Choice D) would lead to hyperthyroidism and laboratory findings of an increased serum concentration of TSH, as well as thyroid hormone. Educational Objective: Graves disease is an autoimmune hyperthyroid condition caused by thyroid-stimulating antibodies that activate the TSH receptor. Overproduction of thyroid hormone causes signs and symptoms of weight loss, insomnia, palpitations, heat intolerance, warm skin, tremor, diaphoresis, and pretibial myxedema. The presence of thyroid eye disease, characterized by exophthalmos, lid lag, and restrictive strabismus, is highly suggestive of Graves disease. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 2807-g (6-lb 3-oz) newborn has a strong cry immediately after delivery. She was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy and a spontaneous vaginal delivery complicated by a few decelerations . The newborn was suctioned at the perineum and placed on the warmer/resuscitation table . After 10 seconds of warming , the newborn's pulse is greater than 100/min, and respirations are 20/min . Examination shows peripheral cyanosis and minimal movement of the upper and lower extremities . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: The initiation of breathing following delivery is crucial for the newborn. A substantial portion of neonates require assistance with the initiation of breathing. Initial, universal steps after delivery include an assessment of the newborn's heart and respiratory rates, muscle tone, reflexes, and color, and immediate warming, drying, and tactile stimulation, all of which are helpful for stimulating spontaneous respirations. Neonates who fail to respond to gentle tactile stimulation should be immediately supported with more invasive support techniques, such as bag and mask ventilation or endotracheal intubation. Tactile stimulation and oxygen therapy are noninvasive and are therefore an appropriate initial step.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Naloxone therapy (Choice B) may be useful for the immediate reversal of opioid toxicity in neonates. This neonate does not have any known risk factors for opioid toxicity and tactile stimulation is a more appropriate next step. Subcutaneous epinephrine therapy (Choice C) is useful for the treatment of anaphylaxis. This newborn has no exposure to agents likely to cause anaphylaxis, the most common of which is a food allergy. Epinephrine is appropriate for newborns with bradycardia in the setting of neonatal resuscitation. Positive-pressure ventilation via face mask (Choice D) and immediate intubation (Choice E) are both appropriate next steps if the newborn remains apneic and does not respond to initial efforts of tactile stimulation. However, these methods are both invasive and are not appropriate first steps. Educational Objective: Many neonates require assistance with the initiation of spontaneous respirations. Tactile stimulation and oxygen therapy are noninvasive and decreases neonatal morbidity and mortality. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A previously healthy 6-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of progressive hair loss over the past 4 weeks . Examination shows a swollen and purulent area on the scalp. A photograph is shown . The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Tinea capitis is a fungal infection of the scalp common in children. The most common presentation is scaly patches with alopecia. The patches of alopecia may demonstrate black dots that represent broken hairs. When a significant inflammatory response to the fungal infection occurs, a kerion develops. A kerion is a boggy and swollen lesion on examination. Tinea capitis is caused by dermatophytes including Trichophyton rubrum, Epidermophyton floccosum, and Microsporum canis. First-line treatment of tinea capitis is with an oral antifungal, usually griseofulvin or terbinafine. Close contacts of patients should be examined as the condition is contagious and can be spread through fomites, such as shared combs, pillows, or hats.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Topical corticosteroid therapy (Choice A) will worsen tinea capitis by inhibiting the inflammatory response necessary to eliminate the infection. Superficial dermatophyte infections treated with topical corticosteroids may become more severe. Tinea treated with topical corticosteroids is often referred to as tinea incognito, because of the severe and unusual morphologies that these infections take on after treatment with topical corticosteroids. Tinea capitis is a fungal infection, not a bacterial infection, and thus oral antibacterial therapy (Choice B) is unnecessary. Tinea capitis and kerion may become secondarily colonized with skin flora, such as S. aureus, in which case antibiotics may be necessary, but this is atypical. Oral antibacterial therapy is appropriate for bacterial skin infections including cellulitis, erysipelas, and severe folliculitis. Surgical excision (Choice D) is unnecessary as the infection can be treated with oral antifungals. In children, dermatologic surgical excision is generally reserved for neoplastic processes. No intervention necessary (Choice E) is not the standard of care for tinea capitis. Without appropriate antifungal treatment, the infection and inflammatory response will worsen. Inadequate treatment puts the patient's close contacts at risk for developing the infection as well. Educational Objective: Tinea capitis is a fungal infection of the scalp common in children. When a significant inflammatory response to the fungal infection occurs, a kerion develops. First-line treatment of tinea capitis includes an oral antifungal, usually griseofulvin or terbinafine, along with the treatment of close contacts, if necessary. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A full-term 24-hour-old newborn has respiratory distress and seizures . Apgar scores were 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes , respectively . An x-ray of the chest shows diffuse hazy infiltrates bilaterally. Leukocyte count is 12,500/mm 3 (65% segmented neutrophils and 10% bands) . Examination of cerebrospinal fluid shows 4 leukocytes/mm 3 (90% lymphocytes) , a glucose concentration of 75 mg/dL , and a protein concentration of 25 mg/dl. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Neonatal sepsis is categorized often on the basis of time from parturition, since the period of time in which symptoms begin may indicate which pathogen is likely involved, thereby guiding therapy. Early-onset neonatal sepsis (within 72 hours of birth) is marked by symptoms of lethargy, seizures, poor feeding, weak cry, and hypotonia. It presents with tachycardia, tachypnea, occasionally fever, and often with an examination that is nonfocal. If examination findings are present, they may reflect the source of infection or may reflect complications of sepsis such as neonatal respiratory distress syndrome. Early-onset neonatal sepsis generally occurs as a result of pathogens acquired from the mother, either through hematogenous or transplacental spread or, commonly, contact acquisition in the birth canal. The most common pathogens associated with early-onset neonatal sepsis include Streptococcus agalactiae (group B), Escherichia coli, coagulase-negative Staphylococcus, and Listeria monocytogenes. Syndromes of serious bacterial infection include bacteremia, meningitis, and pneumonia. Late-onset neonatal sepsis (presenting 72 hours or more after birth) more commonly occurs from environmental pathogens in addition to those acquired from the mother. Pneumonia is more common in early-onset sepsis, and presents with cough, tachypnea, tachycardia, hypoxia, increased work of breathing, and rhonchi on auscultation. Workup for any suspected case of sepsis in a child younger than 30 days of age is broad, and should include a complete blood count, urinalysis, blood cultures, chest x-ray, and lumbar puncture at a minimum, since symptoms in this population are vague and nonspecific, limiting the utility of the history and physical examination to guide workup. X-rays in neonatal pneumonia disclose focal or diffuse airspace disease or may show diffuse interstitial infiltrates suggestive of respiratory distress syndrome. Treatment includes broad-spectrum antibiotics to cover the common pathogens.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Meconium aspiration (Choice B) occurs when the fetus inhales meconium into the lungs and is a known complication of labor and delivery. It presents with signs of respiratory distress (eg, cough, tachypnea, hypoxia, use of accessory muscles of respiration) and severity is a function of the volume of meconium aspirated. It is generally self-resolving when occurring in small amounts; large aspirations can lead to pneumonia or aspiration pneumonitis. Pneumococcal meningitis (Choice C) most commonly occurs in adults, whereas common pathogens causing meningitis in the neonate include Streptococcus agalactiae (group B), E. coli, coagulase-negative Staphylococcus, and L monocytogenes. Pneumocystis jiroveci (formerly P. carini1) pneumonia (Choice D) generally occurs in immunocompromised persons and was seen commonly in individuals with advanced HIV prior to the use of prophylactic antibiotics. Patients classically present with cough, fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypoxia, with rhonchi on lung auscultation and prominent perihilar and multifocal infiltrates on chest x-ray. It would be rare in a neonate. Respiratory syncytial virus pneumonia (Choice E) is one of the most common causes of bronchiolitis and pneumonia in children younger than 2 years of age. In the neonatal period, bacterial infection is more common and is also more consistent with bandemia and diffuse infiltrates on x-ray. Educational Objective: Common causes of early neonatal sepsis include Streptococcus agalactiae (group B), E. coli, and L monocytogenes, which are generally acquired during birth from the mother. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: An 18-month-old boy has had cough, coryza , vomiting , and diarrhea for 5 days and pallor and lethargy for 1 day. His mother states that his urine output has decreased , and the urine is now dark red. He responds poorly to stimuli. He has a grade 3/6 systolic murmur with a gallop and diffuse abdominal tenderness . Laboratory studies show: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Hematocrit Platelet count Serum Na+ Cl· K+ HCO3- Creatinine Urea nitrogen 24% 30,000/mm 3 138 mEq/L 118 mEq/L 6.5 mEq/L 15 mEq/L 2.6 mg/dL 60 mg/dL Hemolytic-uremic syndrome (HUS) is typically associated with infection from enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli O157:H? caused by the production of Shiga toxin. It classically presents in children with bloody diarrhea accompanied by microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury. Other pathogenic precipitants include S. pneumoniae, Salmonella species, and Shigel/a species infections. This patient presents following several days of respiratory and gastrointestinal symptoms, suggesting a bacterial or viral trigger. The abrupt change of pallor and lethargy, along with red urine and falling urine output suggests the presence of both anemia and renal failure. Physical examination may show petechiae, purpura, or ecchymosis, all of which are signs of thrombocytopenia. Laboratory evaluation demonstrates thrombocytopenia, increased creatinine and blood urea nitrogen concentrations, and often multiple electrolyte derangements depending on the extent of volume depletion and acute renal failure. Treatment is supportive and may include plasma exchange; many cases self-resolve. Generally, platelet transfusion is contraindicated because of the risk for worsening the degree of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia since platelet administration has been postulated to worsen the degree of thrombosis. If fever and neurologic symptoms are concomitantly present along with the anemia, thrombocytopenia, and renal failure, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura is diagnosed.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Goodpasture syndrome (Choice A) is a type II (complement-mediated cytotoxic) hypersensitivity reaction that involves autoimmune deposition of lgG against the basement membrane in the lung and kidney. Patients present with hemoptysis and nephritic syndrome, which may be rapidly progressive and cause renal failure or death if not treated. Henoch-Schonlein nephritis (Choice C) is a vasculitis that classically presents in a child with renal failure and palpable purpura on the lower extremities following an upper respiratory infection. Patients often complain of arthralgias and abdominal pain, and intussusception is a known complication. Postinfectious glomerulonephritis (Choice D) is a nephritic syndrome presenting with gross or microscopic hematuria, peripheral or periorbital edema, and hypertension in a child, typically two weeks after infection with group A ~-hemolytic streptococci. Laboratory evaluation may show low serum C3 concentrations and positive anti-streptolysin O and anti-DNase titers. Systemic vasculitis (Choice E) describes a broad class of diseases that encompass small, medium, and large arterial inflammation affecting various organ systems, commonly the kidney, gastrointestinal tract, and lung. While vasculitides may present following illness, the classic triad of anemia, thrombocytopenia, and renal failure makes HUS a more likely diagnosis. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the physician for a well-child examination . He is active and has been healthy except for an episode of otitis media 3 weeks ago treated with amoxicillin. His parents emigrated from Vietnam . His diet consists mainly of fruits and vegetables ; he occasionally eats fish and chicken but no red meat. Examination shows no abnormalities . Laboratory studies show : Hemoglobin Mean corpuscular volume Leukocyte count Platelet count Red cell distribution width 10 g/dL 64 µm 3 6100/mm 3 225,000/mm 3 10% (N=13%-15%) A blood smear is shown . Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's anemia?
correctExplanation: This asymptomatic child with mild anemia, microcytosis, and low red cell distribution width (RDW) who is of southeast Asian heritage most likely has either a- or ~-thalassemia minor. Thalassemia is characterized by the decreased synthesis of globin chains. Normal adult hemoglobin is known as HbA (a~2l and is composed of two a-globin chains and two ~-globin chains. There are four a-globin alleles and two ~-globin alleles. Mutations in one or two a-globin alleles or one ~-globin allele causes thalassemia minor. Thalassemia trait is common in southeast Asia and commonly presents with mild microcytic anemia. Supportive features include the presence of target cells on peripheral blood smear (pictured in the photomicrograph), a low RDW (which indicates that most erythrocytes are of the same size with little variation), and persistence of microcytosis. Iron concentrations can be measured to rule out iron deficiency. Other cell lines including platelets and white blood cells should be within normal ranges. Hemoglobin electrophoresis can be used to distinguish between a- and ~-thalassemia minor. There is no treatment required for thalassemia minor as the resultant anemia is usually not severe.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Antibiotic-induced autoimmune hemolysis (Choice A) can occur after exposure to penicillins and cephalosporins, but the onset is typically acute and occurs within hours to days. While hemolysis can occur weeks later, it is less common. Additionally, patients would be expected to present with normocytic anemia and unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Haptoglobin concentrations can be measured and will be low, while the reticulocyte count will typically be increased. Iron deficiency (Choice C) is a common cause of anemia in menstruating women, strict vegans or vegetarians, and those with chronic gastrointestinal bleeding or celiac disease. It commonly presents with microcytosis, although often with a mean corpuscular volume (MCV) that is higher than what is seen in thalassemia, and an increased RDW indicating the release of premature erythrocytes from the bone marrow. The measurement of serum iron and ferritin, which will be low, are used to make the diagnosis. Transient postinfectious bone marrow suppression (Choice D) may occur following viral infections, but more commonly presents with leukopenia, which is not present in this case. In patients with sickle cell disease, infection with parvovirus B19 can cause a transient aplastic crisis and severe anemia. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A ?-month-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 3-day history of fever and cough. She was born at term following an uncomplicated delivery. She was treated for acute otitis media at 5 months of age. She takes no medications . Immunizations are up-to-date . She appears ill. She is at the 50th percentile for length and 25th percentile for weight. Her temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), pulse is 140/min, respirations are 80/min , and blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 80%. Several 0.5- to 1.5-cm, mobile lymph nodes are palpated in the anterior cervical chain, axillae , and groin. Examination shows white plaques on the buccal mucosa . Diffuse crackles are heard bilaterally. The spleen tip is palpated 2 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory studies show: Leukocyte count 10,500/mm 3 Segmented neutrophils 66% Lymphocytes 30% Monocytes 4% Bronchoalveolar lavage shows Pneumocystis jiroveci (formerly P carini1). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: HIV infection acquired via vertical transmission in the perinatal period is the most likely diagnosis in this patient with oral thrush, diffuse lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, and Pneumocystis pneumonia. HIV transmission may occur at any time during gestation but is most commonly acquired at or around the time of delivery and in the immediate postpartum period when children are breastfeeding. Transmission is uncommon if the mother is taking antiretroviral therapy and has a low HIV viral load. As a result of universal screening for HIV in most developed countries, the incidence of perinatal and pediatric HIV has decreased, although this is not true around the world. Most patients present within the first few months of birth with recurrent pneumonia or opportunistic infections. AIDS-defining illnesses in children are numerous but include P jiroveci pneumonia, as in this patient. Initial evaluation should include measurement of the HIV viral load with concomitant testing for mutations. While this patient should receive treatment for her P jiroveci pneumonia and thrush, she should also be started on antiretroviral therapy once an HIV infection is confirmed.
incorrectExplanation: nd I. Chediak-Higashi syndrome (Choice A) is caused by mutations in the lysosomal trafficking regulator gene (L YST) essential for normal formation and transportation of lysosomes within the cell. It presents with frequent bacterial infections, oculocutaneous albinism, peripheral neuropathy, and progressive neurologic dysfunction. Chronic granulomatous disease (Choice B) is caused by NADPH oxidase deficiency and results in impaired intracellular killing of pathogens. This presents as recurrent pyogenic infections with catalase-positive organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus with normal concentrations of leukocytes and immunoglobulins. Complement deficiency (Choice C), particularly of the terminal complement cascade, typically presents with recurrent infections with Neisseria species. Hyperimmunoglobulinemia E syndrome (Choice E) is caused by mutations in the JAK-STAT signaling cascade, which impairs the development and function of T helper 17 cells (Th n). Patients present with recurrent skin infections, noninflamed abscesses (cold abscesses), and diffuse atopic dermatitis. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A previously healthy 16-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her parents 1 day after she fainted during soccer practice . Her teammates said that she fell to the ground while running and appeared to be unconscious for approximately 15 seconds ; no abnormal movements were noted. There is no prior history of syncope , palpitations , or murmurs . Her parents are concerned because a maternal cousin died suddenly at the age of 22 years of an unknown cause . The patient is alert and oriented . Her vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows no abnormalities . Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.E: Admission to the hospital for observation

correctExplanation: An ECG should be obtained in this patient with unexplained exertional syncope. There are several high-risk cardiac conditions that can present with syncope in pediatric patients, and these can be classified as structural defects, including hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, coronary artery anomalies, or valvular aortic stenosis, or can be a result of electrical abnormalities, such as long QT syndrome or Brugada syndrome. Evaluation with ECG is mandatory in all patients with unexplained syncope. Of these, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is one of the more common causes of syncope. It is generally inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion and may be the cause of death in this patient's cousin. Syncope occurs as a result of left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction with a consequent decrease in cardiac output leading to decreased cerebral perfusion and syncope. Decreased perfusion of the coronary arteries can cause angina and increase the risk for ventricular arrhythmias, although this is not always seen. ECG classically demonstrates left ventricular hypertrophy with non-specific T wave abnormalities in the precordial leads. Deep, narrow, symmetric Q waves may also be seen in the lateral and inferior leads. Echocardiography should be subsequently performed to evaluate the underlying cardiac anatomy, which would allow for assessment of the degree of LVOT obstruction, if present.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Reassurance (Choice A) is inappropriate. Patients with unexplained exertional syncope are at a high-risk for sudden cardiac death. ECG is a low-cost and noninvasive means of assessing for underlying cardiac defects and should be performed as soon as possible. Chest x-ray (Choice B) could be considered in patients with exertional shortness of breath, wheezing, or a prodrome suggestive of bacterial pneumonia, but this patient's presentation is more consistent with a cardiac cause of syncope. EEG (Choice D) is not necessary as this patient's syncopal episode was not associated with classic seizure-like activity. Often, seizures that result in syncope are preceded by an aura, and patients are typically confused upon waking, which is known as a postictal state. The patient's history is not consistent with a seizure. Convulsions can also be seen during syncope. Admission to the hospital for observation (Choice E) is not necessary. Had the patient not regained consciousness or required cardiopulmonary resuscitation, admission to the hospital would be appropriate. This patient should be advised not to participate in exercise until a complete evaluation has been undertaken, but this can be performed in the outpatient setting. Educational Objective: Exertional syncope is a characteristic feature of several high-risk cardiac conditions, including hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. After patient stability is documented, the next step in evaluation should include ECG, which classically demonstrates left ventricular hypertrophy and nonspecific T wave abnormalities. ECG can also help to diagnose conditions such as long QT syndrome or Brugada syndrome, which are other potential causes of cardiac syncope. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A previously healthy 14-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of a 6-week history of right knee pain. She plays volleyball for her school , and the pain is worse after jumping or running . There is no history of trauma . She appears well. Examination shows a tender right knee; there is crepitance with flexion . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Patellofemoral instability is a common cause of anterior knee pain, which is caused by an anatomical defect leading to excessive movement of the patella. It is exacerbated by overuse and activities that put weight on a flexed knee, such as running and jumping. On examination, passive movement of the patella demonstrates increased sliding of the patella in either the lateral axis or superior-inferior axis. The patella may also be tender to palpation. The mainstay of treatment for patellar instability is activity modification and physical therapy. The goal of physical therapy is to strengthen the surrounding muscles and recruit stability of the patella from these muscles, as well as improve the position and balance of the limb overall. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) may also be prescribed for use as needed.
incorrectExplanation: nd I. Conversion disorder (Choice A), called functional neurologic disorder, involves neurologic symptoms such as sensory or motor dysfunction that are not explained by objective findings on physical examination or imaging. Though the symptoms disrupt daily life, patients with functional neurologic disorder may or may not be preoccupied with their symptoms. This patient's symptoms are not solely neurologic. Dermatomyositis (Choice B) is an autoimmune connective tissue disease that causes pink papules over the dorsal fingers (Gottron papules), pink to light purple patches over the upper eyelids (heliotrope sign), light pink to lilac colored patches with telangiectasias on the upper back and sun-exposed chest, dilated capillaries with dropout on the proximal nail folds, and proximal muscle weakness. Growing pains (Choice C) are recurrent, self-limited pains in the extremities that occur during childhood and early adolescence. Physical examination is normal. Juvenile rheumatoid arthritis (Choice D), or systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis, is characterized by fever, arthritis, an evanescent salmon-colored rash, and lymphadenopathy. Legg-Calve-Perthes disease (Choice E) is an idiopathic avascular necrosis of the femoral head, which often presents in young males. The classic presentation includes a slow onset of hip pain that is worsened by activity and associated with a limp. The pain may or may not be relieved with rest. Neuroblastoma with bone marrow metastases (Choice F) is a malignancy of neuroendocrine cells associated with the sympathetic nervous tissue. Bone marrow metastases classically cause pain at night, and the patient would likely appear ill and cachectic. Septic arthritis (Choice H) results from a bacterial infection of the synovial joint space, most commonly by Staphylococcus aureus. The affected joint demonstrates pain, swelling, and erythema. Arthrocentesis is indicated for the evaluation of monoarticular erythema and swelling to evaluate for septic arthritis, which characteristically discloses purulent synovial fluid with >50,000 leukocytes/mm 3. Transient synovitis (Choice I) is a noninfectious arthropathy that presents with joint pain, often the hip, frequently following a viral infection in a child. It is unlikely in this adolescent athlete whose knee pain is chronic and related to activity. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 1-day-old, 1400-g (3-lb 2-oz) newborn has tachypnea , expiratory grunting, flaring of the alae nasi, and peripheral edema. He is cyanotic while breathing room air. Laboratory studies show: Arterial blood gas analysis on room air shows: Which of the following is the most likely acid-base disorder?

choices.D: Respiratory acidosis complicated by renal failure

correctExplanation: Serum Na+ Cl· K+ HCO3- Urea nitrogen Urine pH Protein RBC WBC pH Pco2 Po2 138 mEq/L 100 mEq/L 4.2 mEq/L 14 mEq/L 12 mg/dL 6.2 1+ 0-1/hpf 0-1/hpf 7.17 50 mm Hg 40 mm Hg This patient's laboratory and arterial blood gas evaluation demonstrates a mixed respiratory and anion-gap metabolic acidosis. The metabolic acidosis is indicated by a pH less than 7.35 (acidemia) with decreased HCO3-. Anion gap ([Na•] - {[Cl·]+ [HCO 3·])) calculates unmeasured anions in serum that are contributing to acidity; in this case, the anion gap is increased to 24. Causes of anion gap metabolic acidosis include the ingestion of methanol, propylene glycol, salicylates {late phase), or ethylene glycol, along with uremia, diabetic ketoacidosis, isoniazid use, and lactic acidosis. In this case, a lactic acidosis secondary to inadequate perfusion of organs and forced anaerobic metabolism is likely the cause of the metabolic acidosis as a result of hypoxemia. If functioning correctly, the respiratory system compensates for the acidosis by increasing minute ventilation, which eliminates carbon dioxide, an acid. This results in a decreased pCO2 and an increased pH to approximately normal range. This patient's increased pCO2 suggests that respiratory compensation is not only inadequate but that there is also a concomitant respiratory acidosis. The Winters formula is used to determine the range of pCO2 if compensation is adequate: 1.5(HCO 3 ·) + 8 +/- 2. In this case, the range of pCO2o if adequately compensated, would be 27 to 31 mmHg. The measured pCO2 of 50 mmHg, outside this range, indicates an accumulation of pCO2 in addition to organic anions.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Both lactic acidosis with respiratory compensation {Choice A) and pure metabolic acidosis {Choice B) would demonstrate a metabolic acidosis with a measured pCO2 within the range predicted by the Winters formula. In this case, the measured pCO2 is well above that predicted range, thus respiratory compensation is not adequately occurring and CO2o an acid, is accumulating. Respiratory acidosis and metabolic compensation {Choice C) would present with acidemia, an increased pCO2o and an increased HCO3- concentration. In contrast, this patient has a decreased HCO3- concentration. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department 10 minutes after a firecracker accident ; he has pain and tearing of the right eye. The right eye appears normal. Both pupils are equally round and accommodate to light. His visual acuity is 20/20 . Ocular movements are full. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the eye pain?
correctExplanation: Loss of corneal epithelium describes the pathogenesis of a corneal abrasion, sustained in this example from debris scattered into the eye from a firecracker explosion. Corneal abrasions classically present with pain, conjunctival injection, tearing, and foreign body sensation. Visual acuity may be diminished, and blurry vision may be reported if the abrasion involves the visual axis. If the abrasion is large enough, it may be grossly visible as a discontinuity in the surface of the cornea, but if it cannot be clearly visualized, the use of fluorescein stain and blacklight or slit lamp may be required to detect the epithelial defect, which will be visible as an area of concentrated fluorescein stain, often in a linear or geometric pattern. Treatment includes irrigation to clear any residual debris, analgesia, and prophylactic ophthalmic antibiotic ointment to prevent superimposed infection.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Increased intraocular pressure (Choice A) describes a common finding in glaucoma. In children, this may be a result of congenital glaucoma, which presents with characteristic findings including buphthalmos (an enlarged eye), a large cornea, which may be edematous and opacified, and increased intraocular pressure. Infants typically present with epiphora, photophobia, and blepharospasm or eye rubbing. Inflammation of periorbital tissues (Choice B) describes the pathophysiology of periorbital cellulitis, which presents with erythema, pain, and induration of the eyelids or adjacent skin. The globe itself is not affected. Obstruction of the lacrimal duct (Choice D) presents with tearing (epiphora) from the ipsilateral eye, though it is generally not painful unless the obstructed lacrimal duct is also infected (eg, dacryocystitis). Retinal detachment (Choice E) can occur in the setting of ocular trauma; however, it is generally painless and is accompanied by visual symptoms of photopsia, floaters, and often with a visual field defect. Educational Objective: Corneal abrasions arise as a result of injury to the surface epithelium of the cornea and are diagnosed on gross examination or with the use of fluorescein and a blacklight. Treatment includes irrigation, analgesia, and topical antibiotics. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A previously healthy 1-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of a 3-day history of cough and difficulty breast-feeding . Her mother is concerned because the patient's face turns red when she coughs . She was born at term following an uncomplicated pregnancy , labor, and delivery. She is otherwise healthy. Her mother has had a similar cough for 3 weeks . The patient appears thin. Her temperature is 37.8°C (100°F) , pulse is 110/min, and respirations are 45/min . Examination shows moist mucous membranes and clear rhinorrhea. During the examination , she has a long series of single coughs ending with a loud, high-pitched inhalation . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Episodes of severe paroxysmal coughing in the setting of a respiratory illness is concerning for pertussis. Pertussis occurs as a result of an infection from Bordetella pertussis and classically presents in three stages. The catarrhal stage is first, which presents with fever, rhinorrhea, and a mild cough. This progresses to the paroxysmal stage after 1 to 2 weeks, in which patients experience violent bouts of extreme coughing, at times violent enough to cause secondary traumatic injury such as rib fractures, urinary incontinence, and pneumothorax. Often, such coughing fits are accompanied by cyanosis and may be followed by syncope, emesis, or apnea. The characteristic noise at the end of the cough is responsible for the colloquial name, whooping cough. The paroxysmal stage can last for weeks to months. Symptoms resolve during the convalescent stage, which lasts from 1 to 4 weeks. Pertussis toxin is a major virulence factor that inactivates the G; subunits of G protein-coupled receptors in the respiratory epithelium and systemically, leading to uninhibited adenylyl cyclase activity and increased intracellular cAMP concentrations. In neutrophils and macrophages, this results in impaired recruitment, migration, and production of inflammatory mediators. Pertussis can be prevented with immunization in the form of acellular pertussis, typically administered along with tetanus and diphtheria vaccines (DTaP), but the first dose is not given until 2 months of age. This patient likely acquired the infection from her mother.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Acute bronchiolitis (Choice A) is often the result of infection with respiratory syncytial virus and is likely to present with fever, tachypnea, rhinorrhea, and wheezing. Patients may also display apneic episodes, but severe paroxysms of coughing would be atypical. Chlamydia! pneumonia (Choice B) is commonly preceded by neonatal conjunctivitis. It classically presents in infants with a staccato cough, in which each cough is separated by a brief inspiration. Physical examination may also show tachypnea and crackles. Foreign body aspiration (Choice C) symptoms depend on the size of the aspirated item and its location in the bronchial tree. It can present with respiratory distress and stridor, a high-pitched sound caused by turbulent airflow through obstructed or narrowed upper airway structures, such as the pharynx, larynx, or trachea. Viral laryngotracheobronchitis (Choice E), also known as croup, typically presents with fever, rhinorrhea, a barking cough, and inspiratory stridor. It is commonly secondary to a viral infection from parainfluenza virus. Educational Objective: Pertussis occurs as a result of an infection from Bordetella pertussis and may lead to severe paroxysmal coughing, which may be accompanied by cyanosis and followed by syncope, emesis, or apnea. Pertussis can be prevented with immunization, although this patient is too young to receive the immunization and likely acquired the infection from her mother. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 12-year-old girl is brought to the physician for a well-child examination . She has no history of serious illness. Immunizations are up-to-date . Menarche has not occurred . She is not sexually active . Her mother asks if her daughter should receive the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine . She is reluctant to give permission to administer the vaccine if her daughter is not at risk for infection . The patient and her mother should be advised that which of the following is the most appropriate timing for the patient to receive the HPV vaccine?

choices.C: Immediately after she becomes sexually active
choices.D: At the time of her first Pap smear
choices.E: The vaccine is not indicated if she and her future sexual partners use condoms

correctExplanation: Because about 80% of people will be infected by HPV in their lifetime, the HPV vaccine should be administered to all patients. The vaccine should be administered at age 11 to 12 years, since the immune response is most robust before the teenage years and the onset of sexual activity may occur during the teenage years. HPV is sexually transmitted and is associated with genital warts along with premalignant and malignant lesions of the cervical, anogenital, and oropharyngeal regions. HPV vaccines have significantly decreased the incidence and prevalence of HPV and protect against HPV-related malignancies such as cervical and anal squamous cell carcinoma.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Menarche (Choice B) is unrelated to vaccine efficacy. The vaccine should be given to patients at age 11 to 12 years because of immune response patterns and the onset of sexual behavior, which are not associated with the timing of menarche. The vaccine should be administered to all patients regardless of risk factors such as sexual activity or condom use (Choices C and E) to promote herd immunity. Giving the vaccine after the onset of sexual activity would not protect patients from HPV infection, and condoms decrease but do not eliminate the risk for HPV transmission. The first Pap smear is recommended at age 21 years (Choice D). By age 21, many patients have initiated sexual activity and may already be infected with HPV. HPV infection typically occurs years before concerning cervical lesions may be detected by Pap smear. Educational Objective: HPV is a common sexually transmitted infection that increases the risk for cervical and anogenital cancer. Vaccination against HPV is recommended for all patients at age 11 to 12 years, since the immune response is most robust before the teenage years and the onset of sexual activity may occur during the teenage years. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 10-year-old boy with sickle cell disease is brought to the physician because of a 2-day history of increasing fatigue and shortness of breath . He has had a persistent upper respiratory tract infection for 5 days that has been unresponsive to over-the-counter medications . His temperature is 39.5°C (103.1 °F), pulse is 120/min, respirations are 28/min , and blood pressure is 80/55 mm Hg. Examination shows pale conjunctivae and dry mucous membranes . Cardiac examination shows an active precordium ; a grade 3/6, systolic ejection murmur is heard along the left sternal border. His hematocrit is 16%. Which of the following is most likely to be increased in this patient?
correctExplanation: Cardiac output is most likely to be increased in this patient with severe anemia secondary to sickle cell disease (SCD). Adequate oxygen delivery to peripheral tissues occurs in several steps: oxygenation of the lung alveoli, binding of oxygen to hemoglobin in erythrocytes, and delivery of oxygenated erythrocytes to peripheral tissues with an adequate cardiac output. Peripheral oxygen delivery is mathematically defined by the product of the cardiac output and the arterial oxygen content. Arterial oxygen content is significantly lower in the setting of severe anemia, as in this patient, because there is a substantially lower hemoglobin content. As such, cardiac output must increase to accommodate a substantially lower arterial oxygen content if oxygen delivery to the peripheral tissues is to remain the same. This phenomenon accounts for the patient's active precordium and grade 3/6 systolic ejection murmur. Additionally, this patient likely suffers from a component of sepsis given his persistent upper respiratory tract infection and fever, which would increase the patient's risk for concomitant septic shock. In the early stages of septic shock, the cardiac output is also increased in an attempt to maintain mean arterial pressure.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Central venous pressure (CVP) (Choice B) is likely to be decreased in this patient, who has evidence of dehydration including dry mucous membranes. CVP is often used as a surrogate for preload and correlates with the volume of the right atrium, provided the pulmonary artery pressure is normal. Peripheral tissue oxygenation (Choice C) will either remain the same or decrease further if the patient's cardiac output cannot maintain its increased state and/or the hemoglobin concentration further decreases. Pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) (Choice D) is likely to be normal or low because of the patient's hypovolemia. In older patients with SCD, chronic high-output cardiac states can lead to pulmonary hypertension and increase the PVR. Systemic afterload (Choice E) is likely low or normal in this patient with components of both hypovolemic and septic shock. The patient presents with a severe anemia and evidence of hypovolemia on examination, which would typically result in an increased systemic vascular resistance in an attempt to maintain mean arterial pressure. This patient also presents with a persistent infection and fever, which may indicate a component of concomitant septic shock, which would result in a low systemic vascular resistance from cytokine-mediated arterial vasodilation. Educational Objective: Peripheral oxygen delivery is based on the arterial concentration of hemoglobin and the cardiac output. In states of severe anemia, where the hemoglobin concentration is low, cardiac output must increase in order to compensate, resulting in a high-output cardiac state, as seen in this patient. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A previously healthy 8-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department because of fever, rash, and lethargy for 4 hours. She has had one previous episode of similar symptoms . Her brother died of fulminant meningococcemia 4 years ago. Her temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F), pulse is 128/min, respirations are 32/min , and blood pressure is 95/42 mm Hg. There are scattered purpuric lesions over the trunk and extremities . Her capillary refill time is 4 seconds . Which of the following is the most likely cause?
correctExplanation: Complement system immunodeficiency is the most likely diagnosis in this patient with meningococcemia. Late component complement deficiency (CS to C9) is a common finding in patients who have recurrent infections with Neisseria species, and increases susceptibility to this pathogen through failure to form the membrane attack complex (MAC). Complement activation can occur through the classical, lectin, or alternative pathways, with each pathway converging at the point where C3 is cleaved by C3 convertase, releasing C3a and C3b. Following this, C3b is incorporated into the C3 convertase complex, which subsequently acts on CS convertase to lower the Km (increase the affinity) of CS convertase for its substrate, CS. Cleavage of CS results in the formation of C5a, a potent chemoattractant, and C5b. C5b complexes with C6, C7, CB, and C9 (terminal complement factors) to form the MAC, which allows for the creation of a transmembrane pore that interferes with the integrity of the cellular membrane, leading to cell lysis. Deficiencies of terminal complement factors impair the formation of the MAC and preferentially predispose patients to infection with Neisseria species. While most patients experience mild infection with atypical serotypes, they can also develop fulminant meningococcemia from typical Neisseria serotypes, as in this patient.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. AIDS (Choice A) can develop in pediatric patients who have acquired the infection vertically during the perinatal period from a mother with untreated HIV infection. Most patients present with evidence of recurrent pneumonia, infection with atypical organisms such as Mycobacterium avium, or with opportunistic infections such as Pneumocystis pneumonia. It commonly presents within months of birth but can also develop many years after birth. Child abuse (Choice B) should be suspected in cases where bruising is located in atypical locations such as the back or is with an atypical appearance, such as a linear mark on the upper arm. Purpura on the trunk and extremities is classic for meningococcemia and is far more likely in this patient with sepsis and a family history of meningococcemia. Congenital humoral system immunodeficiency (Choice D) is caused by numerous syndromes, including X-linked agammaglobulinemia, whereby B lymphocyte development is impaired by mutations in the BTK gene. Low or absent immunoglobulin secretion increases the risk for recurrent bacterial infections, but patients present within the first eighteen months of life. Increased susceptibility to Neisseria species, in particular, is not characteristic of this disease. Frequent exposure to multiple pathogens (Choice E) is incorrect. Healthy children are exposed to numerous pathogens on a daily basis and most do not develop invasive bacterial infections. While Neisseria meningitidis is associated with outbreaks in college dorms and military barracks, there is no such history in this case. Vitamin A deficiency (Choice F) is classically associated with xerophthalmia but does not cause the findings described in this patient. Educational Objective: Deficiency of the terminal complement proteins prevents the formation of the MAC, which is a critical component in the complement cascade, typically leading to the formation of a pore in the membrane of pathogenic organisms. Deficiency predisposes to recurrent and invasive infections with Neisseria species. r " , ~ r-- r , Previous

questionStem: A 4-month-old female infant is brought to the physician by her mother for a routine examination . The patient was born at 27 weeks' gestation to a 26-year-old multiparous woman after premature rupture of the membranes and premature labor. The patient's birth weight was 1200 g (2 lb 10 oz), and she spent the first 3 months of her life in the hospital. During hospitalization , she was treated for sepsis and respiratory distress syndrome that required intubation , mechanical ventilation , and umbilical artery catheterization . She is currently receiving oxygen and diuretic therapy at home. She is at the 5th percentile for length and weight. Her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 32/min , and blood pressure is 78/45 mm Hg. Breath sounds are decreased bilaterally, and wheezing is heard occasionally . Cardiac examination shows a pronounced S2 and a precordial heave. Abdominal examination shows hepatomegaly . An ECG shows right axis deviation and right ventricular hypertrophy . Which of the following is the most likely cause of these cardiac findings?
correctExplanation: Pulmonary hypertension is a potential complication of chronic pulmonary disease caused by the response of the pulmonary vasculature to inflammation, hypoxia, and pathologic remodeling. This infant has a history of respiratory distress syndrome requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation and continues to have decreased breath sounds and wheezing. This is consistent with a diagnosis of bronchopulmonary dysplasia, or neonatal chronic lung disease, which is a cause of pulmonary hypertension in infants. As the pulmonary circulation is usually a low-pressure system, the right ventricle is not equipped to pump against such increased pressures.
